Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Define local anesthesia and its appropriate use and technique.
Identify different classifications of local anesthetic medications.
Assess the pharmacology and dosing of local anesthetic classes.
Discuss different additives to local anesthetic agents and advantages of their use.
Review principles of local anesthetic systemic toxicity.
Use of Local Anesthesia
Definition
Local anesthesia is defined as the subcutaneous injection of local anesthetic medication by a
surgeon to block distal nerve endings that innervate tissues in a surgical field.



This differs from peripheral nerve blocks, in which anesthesiologists commonly use
ultrasonographic guidance for blockade of large peripheral nerves in the extremity.
Local anesthesia may be used with or without sedation. An anesthesiologist is not involved in
the post-injection monitoring of the local anesthetic injection and/or resolution of blockade.

Definition
The technique of local anesthesia involves the use of local anesthetic medications by the
surgical team, blocking distal nerve endings that innervate tissues in the surgical field.
Such injection can provide surgical anesthesia for distal procedures not requiring
regional blockade, neuraxial blockade, or general anesthesia. Alternatively, it can be used
as part of postoperative multimodal analgesia for the distal extremity or incisional pain
not covered by a regional blockade dermatome.
Local anesthesia of this type can be administered with or without sedation. This
technique differs from regional anesthesia and peripheral nerve blockade, in which an
anesthesiologist commonly uses ultrasonographic guidance to identify large peripheral
nerves. An anesthesiologist is not commonly involved in this injection intraoperatively,
and anesthesiology acute pain service is not involved in the post-injection monitoring of
the effect and resolution of the blockade. Local anesthesia can be used in combination
with other anesthetic techniques, such as monitored anesthetic care, general anesthesia,
and regional anesthesia1-3 (Resource 1).
Appropriate Use
Surgical anesthesia for distal procedures not requiring regional blockade, neuraxial blockade,
or general anesthesia
Postoperative analgesia for distal extremity or incisional pain not covered by regional blockade
dermatome
Techniques
Digital anesthetic block for hand procedures (Resource 2)

Digital anesthetic block for foot procedures (Resource 3)
Local infiltration of analgesia/periarticular injection
Administered by surgical team at conclusion of a procedure
Does not require monitoring by anesthesiology acute pain service
Depending on the medications used, can provide 6 to 12 hours of postoperative analgesia
Literature is mixed on the advantages compared with other procedures that are part of
multimodal analgesia techniques.
Epidural analgesia is superior to local infiltration analgesia alone in total hip arthroplasty
and total joint arthroplasty in terms of pain scores and opioid use; however, it is not
superior in time to hospital discharge.
Growing data support local infiltration analgesia as part of multimodal analgesia in
combination with peripheral nerve blocks.

Techniques
Specific techniques have been described for the use of local anesthesia. For distal hand
and foot procedures, digital anesthetic block techniques are commonly used. With these
more targeted injections, a patient can be administered surgical anesthesia without a
prolonged peripheral nerve territory motor and sensory blockade.
One common use of local anesthesia is as a digital anesthetic block for distal procedures
of the hand. This can be performed via a dorsal web space block and a volar block.
During a dorsal web space block, a total of approximately 3 mL of local anesthetic
medication is sterilely injected alongside and on top of the extensor tendon and into the
web space on the opposite side of the digit. This provides surgical anesthesia for the
dorsum of the finger. For procedures of the ventral digits, a volar block can be
performed using approximately 5 mL of local anesthetic. Three injections are made, the
first at the palmar midline of the targeted digit at the distal palmar crease. After a
midline injection, two additional injections are made toward the distal radial and distal
ulnar nerves. This will provide surgical anesthesia for distal procedures of the digits of
the hand.4
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116

A similar technique can be used for digital anesthetic blocks of the foot. This block
involves two injections, with one on each side of the metatarsal head on the dorsum of
the foot. For each injection, the needle is advanced until the plantar skin begins to tent,
withdrawn 1 cm, and approximately 3 mL of local anesthetic is injected, with 2 mL
injected during withdrawal of the needle. Surgical anesthesia will be achieved from such
injections, which is useful for distal procedures of the digits of the foot.4 Local anesthesia
also has been safely and effectively used as a surgical anesthetic in several other
orthopaedic procedures, including upper extremity surgery and hip fracture repair in
high-risk patients.5-7
Research on the use of local infiltration of analgesia, or periarticular injection, as part of
a multimodal analgesia regimen for orthopaedic surgery is ongoing. Periarticular
injection technique has been described before cementation during total knee
arthroplasty and before surgical closure8-10 (Video 1).
Video 1: Su EP: Video. Total Knee Replacement Periarticular Injection. New York, NY, 2020.
For total hip arthroplasty, periarticular injection into the anterior and posterior capsules,
the periosteum, and the surrounding musculature has been outlined.8 The composition
of injection varies; however, a combination of different medication classes is used. The
injection typically contains local anesthetic, epinephrine, corticosteroid, opioid,

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
4/24

antibiotic, and normal saline.8,9,11 Depending on the concentrations and medication
classes selected, such injections can provide analgesic benefit for 6 to 12 hours
postoperatively.3
Initial data revealed tremendous benefit to the use of periarticular injection; however,
this benefit was observed with periarticular injection compared with systemic analgesic
agents without coinciding peripheral nerve blockade.3 More recent literature has shown
that postoperative epidural analgesia was superior to periarticular injection alone in
total hip and total knee arthroplasty. Benefits were demonstrated in opioid consumption
and pain with movement; however, no difference in hospital length of stay was
noted.9,11 Emerging data have compared the use of periarticular injection alone to
periarticular injection in combination with peripheral nerve blockade. Studies have
demonstrated benefit for total knee arthroplasty, with a combination of adductor canal
block and periarticular injection leading to decreased pain scores 24 hours
postoperatively; however, hospital length of stay and opioid consumption did not differ
between the groups.8
Characteristics of Local Anesthetic Agents
Overview
The mechanism of all local anesthetic agents is the same: bind to inactive intracellular sodium
channels to block propagation of action potential down axon.
Differences between local anesthetic agents are based on chemical properties of the
medications.

Overview
Local anesthetic medications hinder the transmission of sensory and motor information
via the same mechanism, sodium channel blockade. Under resting conditions, voltage-
gated sodium channels are closed, keeping positively charged sodium ions
extracellularly. After administration, the local anesthetic medication will bind to the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Local Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
5/24

inactive and open voltage–gated sodium channel. This limits additional influx of sodium
intracellularly and blocks the propagation of action potential down an axon.1,2
Onset
Speed of onset related to pKa of medication
A pKa value closer to physiologic pH allows for more an unionized form of drug to be available
to cross lipid membrane.
A higher level of unionized drug will speed onset, with more drug crossing lipid membrane to
act on the intracellular sodium channel.

Onset
Local anesthetic onset of action coincides with one of the basic chemical properties of
the medication, pKa. The pKa determines the ratio of charged and uncharged forms of
the medication that exist at physiologic pH. As weak bases, local anesthetic agents have
a pKa value higher than physiologic pH. The closer the pKa is to physiologic pH, the more
uncharged form of drug will be available to cross the lipid membrane and block
intracellular sodium channels. A greater ratio of uncharged medication administered will
speed onset, with more medication crossing the lipid membrane to block propagation of
action potentials down an axon.1,2,12
Duration
Duration of action related to degree of drug protein binding and lipid solubility
Binding to local proteins allows the drug to remain at the receptor site longer.
Bupivacaine is highly protein bound, with a long duration of action.
High lipid solubility of the drug slows diffusion away from the lipid-rich environment of the cell
membrane to the hydrophilic bloodstream.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Local Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
6/24


Duration
The duration of action of local anesthetic agents is related to the degree of protein
binding that the medication exhibits. With a higher degree of protein binding, local
anesthetic medication will avoid normal metabolism compared with unbound drug and
remain active at receptor sites longer. For example, bupivacaine is a long-acting local
anesthetic agent, partly because of a characteristically high degree of protein binding
(95%). In addition, higher lipid solubility allows for longer duration of action. For more
hydrophilic medications, the lipid-rich environment of the cell membrane creates a
slower diffusion of medication into the hydrophilic blood circulation. Finally, vasoactive
additives to local anesthetic mixtures can prolong duration. Epinephrine commonly is
used to prolong duration, acting to vasoconstrict local circulation to decrease local
anesthetic uptake.1
Potency
Greater lipid solubility leads to greater potency.
Decreased medication dose is necessary to be available to cross lipophilic cell membrane.

Potency
The lipid solubility of a local anesthetic agent also correlates with the potency of that
medication. A greater lipid solubility leads to a greater drug potency, leading to ease of
diffusion into neural tissue.1 With a more hydrophilic medication, a smaller
concentration of medication is necessary to be available to cross the lipid-rich cell
membrane.12
Local Anesthetic Agent Classification
Overview

Mechanism: sodium channel blockade, block propagation of action potential in axon
Composed of lipophilic group, an intermediate chain link, and a hydrophilic group
Intermediate link chain creates difference in classification: amino esters and amino amides

Overview
All local anesthetic agents act via sodium channel blockade, impeding action potential
transmission in nervous tissue. The chemical composition of all local anesthetic
medications also is mostly the same Each medication structure consists of a lipophilic
group, a hydrophilic group, and an intermediate chain link. The intermediate chain link
between the hydrophilic and lipophilic groups creates a difference in local anesthetic
medication classes. Depending on the structure of this link, medications are
characterized as amino-ester or amino-amide local anesthetic agents.1,2,13
Amino Esters
Metabolism in plasma via plasma esterases
Procaine, tetracaine, chloroprocaine
One “i” in the name of esters
More commonly associated with allergic reactions if derivates of para-aminobenzoic acid
(PABA)

Amino Esters
The amino ester group of local anesthetic agents include procaine, tetracaine, and
chloroprocaine. A simple method to recall the medications that belong to this class is in
the name because all amino esters only have one “i” in the spelling of the medication.
Amino esters undergo metabolism independent of the renal or hepatic system because
they are metabolized directly in plasma via plasma esterases. Although rare, this class of
local anesthetic agents is more commonly associated with true patient allergic reactions.
This is because the derivation of some amino ester chemical structures from PABA. PABA

9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Local Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
8/24

has been shown to have allergenic properties, and true local anesthetic allergic reactions
have been associated with this compound.1,12
Procaine
Maximum dose: 8 mg/kg
Moderate duration: 45 to 60 minutes
pKa: 8.9
Commonly used as part of eutectic mixture of local anesthetic (EMLA) cream of 2.5% procaine
and 2.5% lidocaine

Procaine
The most common use of the local anesthetic procaine in modern practice is as part of
EMLA cream. Consisting of a combination of 2.5% procaine and 2.5% lidocaine, EMLA
cream generally is used as a topical local anesthetic before superficial procedures. This is
more commonly used in situations in which patients may not tolerate such procedures,
such as intravenous catheter placement in children. With a pKa of 8.9, procaine has a
moderate onset time, and the duration of action is approximately 45 to 60 minutes. The
maximum dose of procaine recommended to avoid local anesthetic toxicity is 8 mg/kg,
which is considerably greater than the dosage used in EMLA cream application.
Tetracaine
pKa: 8.5
Moderate duration: 45 to 60 minutes
Maximum dose: 3 mg/kg
Not commonly used; high risk for transient neurologic symptoms (TNS)
Self-limiting, moderate to severe pain after spinal anesthesia

Tetracaine
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116

Tetracaine is an amino ester local anesthetic agent that is less commonly used in
modern practice. With a pKa of 8.5, this medication has a moderate onset time, with
solubility and protein binding properties leading to a moderate duration of
approximately 45 to 60 minutes. The maximum dose recommended to avoid local
anesthetic toxicity is 3 mg/kg. The use of tetracaine has fallen out of favor because of
demonstrated high risk of TNS. TNS is a self-limiting condition described after spinal
anesthesia blockade, in which a patient experiences moderate to severe pain and
dysesthesia within the spinal levels blocked. Such symptoms generally present within the
first 24 hours postoperatively, and most symptoms resolve by postoperative day three.12
Chloroprocaine
pKa: 8.7
Associated with fast onset because of availability of high concentration formulations (3%)
Fast offset because of rapid metabolism by plasma esterases
Short duration: 30 to 60 minutes
Commonly used for neuraxial anesthetic agents for short ambulatory procedures
Maximum dose: 12 mg/kg

Chloroprocaine
Although the pKa of chloroprocaine (8.7) is not substantially closer to physiologic pH
compared with other local anesthetic medications, chloroprocaine is associated with a
very fast onset. This is because of the availability of chloroprocaine in high concentration
formulations (3% or 30 mg/mL), allowing for faster onset of medication effect.
Chloroprocaine also has a relatively short duration of action because of rapid
metabolism by plasma esterases. Depending on the dosage used, the duration of
chloroprocaine for spinal and epidural anesthesia blockade is approximately 30 to 60
minutes. The resolution of motor and sensory blockade after neuraxial anesthetic has
been consistently shown to be faster and more predictable than other local anesthetic
medications. Accordingly, this medication commonly is used during neuraxial anesthetic
agents for short, ambulatory procedures of the lower extremity. With a maximum dose

10/24

of 12 mg/kg, chloroprocaine is associated with a low risk for local anesthetic systemic
toxicity (LAST), even with the high concentration formulations available.12,13
Amino Amides
Hepatic metabolism
Prilocaine, lidocaine, mepivacaine, ropivacaine, bupivacaine
Two “i”s in the name of amides
Can produce a true allergic reaction if preparation contains methylparaben, which has a
similar structure to PABA
Use as a preservative has fallen out of favor

Amino Amides
The second major class of local anesthetic medications is amino amides, which have a
characteristically different intermediate link structure compared with amino esters.
Dissimilar from esters, amides undergo hepatic metabolism; therefore, the duration of
action may be prolonged in patients with preexisting liver disease. The simple method to
recall the medications that fall into this class is by recognizing that amino amides have
two “i”s in the spelling of the medication. Amides are less commonly associated with true
allergic reactions compared with amino ester local anesthetic agents. Historically,
amides were linked to patient allergy because of medication preparations containing
methylparaben, which has a similar chemical structure to PABA; however, the use of
methylparaben as a preservative has fallen out of favor, and a true allergic reaction to
amino amide local anesthetic agents is unlikely.1,2
Lidocaine
pKa: 7.9
Maximum dose: 4.5 mg/kg; 7 mg/kg with epinephrine
Moderate duration of action: 60 to 120 minutes
Available in varying concentrations: 0.5% to 5%
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Local Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
11/24

Spinal lidocaine is associated with a high risk for TNS.

Lidocaine
One of the most used local anesthetic agents is lidocaine, especially for short to
moderate duration subcutaneous injection and blockade. With a pKa of 7.9 and close to
physiologic pH, lidocaine has a relatively fast onset compared with most local anesthetic
agents. The duration of action of lidocaine is approximately 60 to 120 minutes, and it is
commonly used for subcutaneous infiltration, short-duration peripheral nerve blockade,
and short to moderate effect in epidural anesthesia. With varying concentration and
formulations from 0.5% to 5%, lidocaine is used not only as injectable medication but
also within topical cream and gel. Lidocaine is no longer used in spinal anesthetic agents
because it has been shown to be associated with a high risk for TNS. The maximum dose
of lidocaine recommended to avoid LAST is 4.5 mg/kg; however, this can be increased to
7 mg/kg with the use of epinephrine as an additive.2,12,13
Mepivacaine
pKa: 7.6 (close to physiologic pH, fast onset)
Moderate duration of 90 to 180 minutes in neuraxial block, 6 to 8 hours in peripheral block
Commonly used for moderate-duration brachial plexus blocks and moderate-duration spinal
anesthesia
Maximum dose: 4.5 mg/kg (7 mg/kg with epinephrine)
Generally used as 1.5%; however, concentrations range from 1% to 3%.
Similar characteristics to lidocaine but very low incidence of TNS

Mepivacaine
A commonly used local anesthetic agent in peripheral nerve blockade and neuraxial
blockade, mepivacaine exhibits a fast onset because of a pKa near physiologic pH of 7.6.
Mepivacaine generally is available in a concentration of 1.5% but also exists in
concentrations ranging from 1% and 3%. The duration of mepivacaine is classified as
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Local Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
12/24

moderate, with a neuraxial duration of action of approximately 90 to 180 minutes and a
peripheral nerve block duration of approximately 6 to 8 hours, depending on the dosage
used. Fast onset and moderate duration enable mepivacaine to be a common option for
moderate-duration brachial plexus blockade and moderate-duration spinal anesthetic
blockade.1,12 Although similar in structure and characteristics to lidocaine, the risk of
TNS associated with mepivacaine has been reported to be much lower in large cohort
studies.14
Ropivacaine
pKa: 8.1
Long duration of action: 240 to 480 minutes
Available as 0.2% to 1%
Maximum dose: 3 mg/kg
Lower risk of cardiac toxicity compared with bupivacaine

Ropivacaine
Ropivacaine, as an amide local anesthetic agent with a characteristically long duration of
action, generally is used for extended peripheral nerve blockade. Sodium channel
blockade can last 4 to 8 hours because ropivacaine is a common option for single-shot
peripheral nerve blocks and continuous peripheral nerve blockade via catheter
placement. Available in concentrations as high as 1%, a concentration of 0.2%
ropivacaine typically is selected for extended peripheral nerve blockade and continuous
infusion. The pKa of ropivacaine is 8.1, leading to a moderate onset time. The maximum
dose recommended for ropivacaine is 3 mg/kg; however, the risk for cardiotoxicity
associated with ropivacaine is lower compared with other long-acting local anesthetic
agents, such as bupivacaine. This may be partially because of a decreased lipid solubility
and ability to create local vasoconstriction and a decreased affinity for cardiac sodium
channels.1,2,12
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Local Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
13/24

Bupivacaine
pKa: 8.1
Long duration of action: 240 to 480 minutes in neuraxial block; 12 to 16 hours in peripheral
block
High lipid solubility and high protein binding
Commonly used for long-duration spinal anesthesia (0.5%), long-duration surgical block
anesthesia (0.5%)
Commonly used in regional blocks for postoperative analgesia (0.25%)
Maximum dose: 2.5 mg/kg
Highest risk for cardiac toxicity because of strong affinity for sodium channels in the heart

Bupivacaine
Bupivacaine is one of the most used local anesthetic agents for subcutaneous injection,
periarticular injection, neuraxial blockade, and peripheral nerve blockade. This is
partially because of its extended duration of action, creating a beneficial addition to
multimodal analgesic therapy regimens. With a pKa of 8.1, the onset is relatively slower
in commonly available concentrations of 0.25% to 0.5% compared with other local
anesthetic medications. A bupivacaine concentration of 0.5% is a frequently used local
anesthetic for long-duration (approximately 4 hours) neuraxial surgical anesthesia and
long-duration (12 to 16 hours) peripheral nerve blockade surgical anesthesia. A lower
concentration of 0.25% is successfully used for extended analgesic peripheral nerve
blockade, and more dilute concentrations ranging from 0.0625% to 0.1% are effective as
analgesic doses via epidural infusion. The extended effect of bupivacaine is because of
its high lipid solubility and its high degree of protein binding of approximately 95%. The
maximum dose of bupivacaine recommended to avoid local anesthetic toxicity is 2.5
mg/kg. Bupivacaine is associated with a higher risk for cardiac toxicity compared with
other local anesthetic agents because of its strong affinity for sodium channels in cardiac
myocytes.1,12,15
In recent years, a novel formulation of bupivacaine has become available and approved
for select indications. The unique structure of liposomal bupivacaine allows for
continued release of medication after single-shot injection for an extended period. In
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Local Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
14/24

liposomal bupivacaine, a lipid bilayer surrounds and encapsulates standard bupivacaine
molecules. This allows for slow release from the lipid containment, after which
medication is free to bind to and block sodium channels.16 Currently, liposomal
bupivacaine is approved by the US FDA for local anesthetic wound infiltration for
postoperative analgesia and for use in interscalene peripheral nerve blockade; it may
have a duration of action of as long as 72 hours.13 Studies have shown that bupivacaine
and liposomal bupivacaine are safe and effective for analgesia in several orthopaedic
surgical procedures, including shoulder arthroplasty and anterior cruciate ligament
repair.17,18 Early literature on liposomal bupivacaine showed great promise compared
with a placebo, with improvement in pain scores and opioid consumption;16 however,
data on the use of liposomal bupivacaine versus standard bupivacaine infiltration have
yet to show substantial benefit. The literature has shown similarities in measures of
postoperative pain, opioid consumption, and hospital length of stay in comparisons of
liposomal bupivacaine with other long-acting local anesthetic agents. No increased risk
of LAST has been reported with the use of liposomal bupivacaine.16,19
Local Anesthetic Additives
Overview
Several additive medications can be added to local anesthetic drugs to prolong the duration of
action.
Advantages of additives include prolonged duration without an increased risk of LAST from
higher doses of local anesthetic drug.

Overview
A large body of literature is available on adjuncts to local anesthetic injections, with data
supporting the ability of various medication classes to prolong block duration. The
advantage of using an additive rather than increased concentrations of a local anesthetic
medication is the prolongation of blockade without increased risk of LAST from
increased local anesthetic dosage. Although the mechanism of block extension is not
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Local Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
15/24

clearly defined for all additives, several medication classes have been studied and
proven beneficial for longer duration of action20 (Resource 4).
Epinephrine
Alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 agonist
Causes local vasoconstriction to limit systemic absorption and metabolism of local anesthetic
drugs
Because of limitation of blood flow to the area of local infiltration, epinephrine increases the
maximum allowable dose for infiltration.
Decreases risk of LAST
Systemic effects of epinephrine also act as sign of intravascular injection.

Epinephrine
Epinephrine is an agonist of alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 receptors. As a
vasoactive medication, it causes local vasoconstriction if used as a local anesthetic
adjunct. This allows for limitation of systemic absorption and metabolism of local
anesthetic medications if used as an additive. Because of this vasoconstriction and
limitation of blood flow to the area of local anesthetic infiltration, epinephrine increases
the maximum allowable dose without an increased risk of toxicity.15 Epinephrine-
induced vasoconstriction also has been shown to improve surgical conditions and
surgical time, particularly during surgical procedures of the hand and upper extremity in
which local, anesthetic-only techniques are used.5,6 This mechanism also can serve as a
marker of systemic injection, with increased heart rate and blood pressure indicating
intravascular injection from the epinephrine additive.2 Typically, epinephrine is added in
concentrations of 5 to 10 μg/mL, or 1:200,000 to 1:400,000. Depending on the local
anesthetic medication epinephrine is used in combination with, epinephrine has been
shown to prolong blocks by 30 to 60 minutes. No block extension benefit has been
shown by the addition of epinephrine to long-acting local anesthetic agents, such as
bupivacaine and ropivacaine.20
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Local Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
16/24

Dexamethasone
Corticosteroid
Low doses (1 to 4 mg) added to local anesthetic agents can prolong peripheral nerve block 12
to 24 hours.

Dexamethasone
Dexamethasone, a corticosteroid, is a common adjunct medication used to prolong the
block duration of local anesthetic injection. A large body of data is available on
dexamethasone as an additive; however, the literature has reported conflicting
information. Prior studies demonstrated prolongation of local anesthetic peripheral
nerve blockade by 12 to 24 hours with the addition of 1 to 4 mg of dexamethasone.
Higher doses of additive have been shown to prolong the duration of the block up to two
times longer than a block with local anesthetic alone; however, evidence suggests that
high-dose intravenous dexamethasone (8 to 10 mg) can extend peripheral block
duration similar to that of perineural dexamethasone used as a local anesthetic additive.
Concern exists with regard to the theoretic neurotoxic effect of perineural
dexamethasone used as an adjunct; however, some data support a potential
neuroprotective effect.20,21
Buprenorphine
Mu opioid receptor partial agonist
Studies have shown systemic opioid-sparing effect for as long as 24 hours if added to local
anesthetic mixture in block.

Buprenorphine
Dissimilar from the risk of sedation that exists with the use of many opioids as
perineural local anesthetic adjuncts, the use of buprenorphine has not been associated
with such systemic adverse effects. As a mu opioid receptor partial agonist,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Local Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
17/24

buprenorphine is an effective additive without the risk associated with other opioid
medications. The literature has shown an opioid consumption sparing for as long as 24
hours if buprenorphine is used as an additive to local anesthetic agents in peripheral
nerve blocks; however, an increased risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting has been
reported with the use of buprenorphine as an additive. Postoperative nausea and
vomiting prophylaxis should be administered in patients in whom this local anesthetic
adjunct is used.20,21
Alpha-2 Agonists
Clonidine has been more thoroughly studied as an additive and can prolong block for several
hours.
Systemic adverse effects, such as hypotension and bradycardia, can occur.
Limited data exist with regard to addition of dexmedetomidine. It may prolong blocks but also
may have more exaggerated systemic adverse effects.

Alpha-2 Agonists
Clonidine, an alpha-2 agonist, has been thoroughly studied as a local anesthetic additive.
The literature has indicated a considerable prolongation of block time, with extension
between 2 and 4 hours. Several trials have indicated successful extension of block time
with long-acting local anesthetic agents, such as ropivacaine and bupivacaine. However,
evidence shows that increasing doses of clonidine used in peripheral blocks cause
systemic adverse effects, such as bradycardia, hypotension, and syncope, related to
alpha-2 agonists.
As a novel, more potent alpha-2 agonist compared with clonidine, emerging research is
being reported on the use of dexmedetomidine as an additive to local anesthetic agents.
Some studies have shown success, with longer block extension times compared with
clonidine; however, data suggest that perineural dexmedetomidine also creates more
pronounced adverse effects observed with alpha-2 agonist use.20,21
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Local Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002116
18/24

Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity
Overview
Mechanism of toxic sodium channel blockade
Progression of symptoms

Overview
Local anesthetic medications block sodium channels in nervous tissue to create a
sensory block for surgical anesthesia and postoperative analgesia. Therefore, LAST
results from excessive local anesthetic dosage, causing widespread blockade of sodium
channels throughout the body. A wide range of clinical presentation of LAST is possible,
ranging from minor symptoms to severe neurologic depression and cardiovascular
collapse.2,15
Neurologic Symptoms
Varied symptomatology
Typically begins with perioral numbness and tingling, tinnitus, vertigo, restlessness, metallic
taste
Progression to somnolence, neurologic depression, seizure

Neurologic Symptoms
Classically, the presenting symptomatology of LAST was associated with a prodrome of
perioral numbness and tingling, tinnitus, vertigo, restlessness, and metallic taste. This
prodrome may, with a varying time course, progress to neuroexcitation and seizure,
somnolence, and neurologic depression;15 however, the literature suggests that this
progression does not occur in most patients. A recent review reported that more than
50% of patients with LAST presented with seizure as the first symptom.22

Cardiovascular Symptoms
In general, less sensitive to local anesthetic toxicity than neurologic symptoms
Hypotension, myocardial depression, dysrhythmia, asystole

Cardiovascular Symptoms
In general, the cardiovascular system is less sensitive to LAST than the nervous system.
With the initial neurotoxicity, a sympathetic surge can cause hypertension and
tachycardia. With increased toxic dosage, local anesthetic agents cause dysrhythmias,
myocardial depression, and cardiovascular collapse. The interference of the normal
cardiac conduction system because of sodium channel blockade may lead to malignant
arrythmias and cardiac arrest.15
Management
Cornerstone of management is intralipid, 20% lipid emulsion that limits the ability of local
anesthetic agents to bind to receptors
Patient weight less than 70 kg: 1.5 mL/kg bolus for 2 to 3 minutes, followed by infusion of
0.25 mL/kg/min
Patient weight higher than 70 kg: 100 mL bolus for 2 to 3 minutes, followed by 200 to 250 mL
infusion for 15 to 20 minutes
Supportive management: airway management, hemodynamic support, seizure control

Management
In combination with the administration of intralipid, patient airway management,
hemodynamic support, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation should occur if necessary.
Benzodiazepines should be administered for seizure control, and epinephrine can be
administered to support hemodynamics; however, in smaller doses compared with
those used during the standard Advanced Cardiac Life Support algorithm (<1 μg/kg
versus 1 mg used in standard Advanced Cardiac Life Support algorithm). Vasoactive
